title: Relief work
hook: Taiwanese Buddhist relief volunteers at disasters around the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Humanistic Buddhism: Buddhism in the human world, in schools, hospitals and offices. Your line was this human life. What kind thing did you do at work? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

A line of volunteers in navy blue and white moves through a town after an earthquake. They carry blankets, rice and hot meals. When one of them hands a blanket to an old man, she uses both hands, and then she bows to him and says thank you. Not you're welcome. Thank you. The man looks surprised. Why is the giver thanking him? That small bow belongs to a Buddhist relief movement from Taiwan, one that tells its own beginning as a handful of coins. Today: relief work.
screen: `NAVY BLUE AND WHITE.` → `A BLANKET, WITH BOTH HANDS.` → `THE GIVER SAYS THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the founder. The movement is called Tzu Chi, which its members translate as compassion and relief. It was founded by a Buddhist nun, Dharma Master Cheng Yen, on Taiwan's east coast. Second, the bamboo tube. The story the movement tells goes like this: she asked a small group of housewives to drop a little coin into a bamboo tube each day, before going to market, to help the poor. A small amount, they asked? Small, she said, but every day. Tradition says that's how it started: not with a big gift but with a daily one. The coins grew into clinics, hospitals and teams of volunteers that now travel to floods, earthquakes and storms far beyond Taiwan. Third, the giving itself. In Buddhism, giving is called dana, a practice anyone can start with. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "let him overcome the greedy by liberality." Tzu Chi volunteers add a twist. They thank the person who receives, because receiving gives the volunteer a chance to practice. That's why the bow. Fourth, what it asks of the volunteer. Volunteers include ordinary lay people: shopkeepers, teachers, retirees. They clean mud out of houses, cook in field kitchens and sort recycling to raise funds. The movement's way of seeing it is that the work is the practice. Not a reward. Not a good deed to boast about. Hands that help, and a mind that stays humble while they do it.
screen: `A NUN NAMED CHENG YEN.` · `A COIN IN A BAMBOO TUBE.` · `OVERCOME THE GREEDY BY LIBERALITY.` · `THE WORK IS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HANDS THAT HELP.`

segments.voice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, if you'd like to try this. Let the breath settle into them. Somewhere in the world a place is hurting right now, after a flood, a fire, a quake or a war. Let it come to mind, and keep breathing gently. Now think of one relief effort you could give to, even a little, the way the housewives gave a coin. If giving money isn't possible, think of time, or a word passed on to someone who can. Choose one. Then sit with the idea of thanking the people you help. The bell holds the time.
Relief work. Buddhist volunteers bringing food, shelter and care after disasters, treating giving as practice and thanking those who receive. Today's word.
Your line: hands that help. Today, give to one relief effort, however small, and if you hand anything to anyone, try using both hands. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Tzu Chi volunteers, founded around the nun Cheng Yen in Taiwan, bring food, shelter and medical care after disasters, often handing aid with both hands and thanking those who receive it.

Navy-and-white uniforms, both-hands giving, and the thank-you bow to recipients: confirm as Tzu Chi practice.
